newsitem.title: USA: Union issue threatens to keep U.S. Senate in town.
newsitem.headline: Union issue threatens to keep U.S. Senate in town.

text.p: An arcane labor issue affecting only one company threatened Monday to hold the Senate in session and dash members' hopes of adjourning for the year as early as Monday night.
The problem centered on a popular bill beefing up airport construction and anti-terrorism measures that all senators wanted enacted.
But pro-labor senators, who had the ability to block the bill at least temporarily, wanted it shorn of a measure that applied just to the Federal Express Corp..

These senators said the provision, quietly inserted into the bill as a technical correction, was designed to help FedEx in "union-busting" efforts. Supporters of the provision said it merely put right an error in earlier legislation.

At issue was whether employees of FedEx were covered by the Railway Labor Act that required them to form a nationwide bargaining unit if they wish to have a union, or the National Labor Relations Act, which allowed local bargaining units.

A bill passed last year left the situation at FedEx ambiguous and the provision in the bill sought to ensure that the firm was covered by the Railway Labor Act, which made union organizing more difficult.

Airline employees are covered by the Railway Labor Act, and FedEx's pilots are unionized. Truck drivers are usually covered by the Labor Relations Act, Sen. Edward Kennedy said. FedEx's drivers are not unionized.
The Massachusetts Democrat attacked the provision in the bill as "a parting shot against American workers in the closing hours of this Congress."
Kennedy said the airports bill could win speedy Senate approval but he said he intended to fight the FedEx provision.

Senate Republican Leader Trent Lott was equally adamant. He said he was ready to file a motion to cut off debate on the bill -- a course that usually would take at least two days to play itself out, although Lott said he still expected to adjourn Monday night or Tuesday night.
"There's no doubt in my mind that this is labor trying to extract one additional pound of flesh from the Congress as we go out the door," Lott told reporters.
Lott would need 60 votes to cut off debate and Kennedy indicated that that he was not yet able to block Lott.
"We're building gathering strength. We haven't taken a head count," he said.

As an alternative route, Kennedy suggested that the Senate could pass a separate resolution striking the FedEx provision and send it to the House, where members have already left town, to be adopted without debate.
In a floor speech Kennedy said that FedEx "is notorious in its anti-union ideology, but there is no need for Congress to become an accomplice in its union-busting tactic."
He said the company's truck drivers in Pennsylvania had been trying to join the United Auto Workers union for two years.
FedEx spokswoman Shirlee Clark said the company needed the provision in the bill to resolve costly legal challenges resulting from ambiguous current law.
She said that a requirement that the firm's "couriers" be organized nationally was needed to prevent labor groups disrupting the firm's integrated air-ground operations.
